newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-"I'm no insider" says Pearson's Scardino.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-"I'm no insider" says Pearson's Scardino.

text.p: Marjorie Scardino, set to head British media company Pearson, denied on Thursday that she was a company insider and said she was prepared to make radical change "if needed".
Scardino's appointment as chief executive to succeed Frank Barlow raised little initial enthusiasm among analysts who had been hoping for a big-name outsider to come in.
Scardino, 49, is chief executive of the Economist Group, 50 percent owned by Pearson, but said she qualified as an outsider.
"I would like to put that one to rest - I am an outsider to Pearson," she said in a telephone interview with Reuters.

Scardino said there was a little-known trust agreement which ensured that Pearson representatives remained in a minority on the board at the Economist. "We jealously guard our independence, we're not a part of the Pearson group," she said.

She said she had spoken to members of the Pearson board and had received assurances that they would not stand in the way of radical change. Asked if she was planning a radical shake-up, she replied "if needed".
Scardino said it was too early for her to say what she planned to do at the company. "Everyone expects me to have my plan all set, but I haven't," she said.
But she was aware of press and market criticism of a lack of management focus at Pearson.
"I tried to read all the clips I could find. That was both illuminating and depressing," she said.
"I know this company has been broken up and put back together (by journalists and analysts) in all kinds of ways. I think I'm aware of all the possibilities."

She received a glowing reference from Economist chairman Dominic Cadbury: "I am sure that she will move quickly to assess the Pearson business and define a new strategic direction which she will set about implementing," he said.
"She is an excellent choice for the job and is extremely well-qualified to take on the responsibility," he added.

"She has the appropriate experience of publishing and a background as a lawyer, as well as knowing the U.S. and British environments first hand, and has a great record of success in the Economist's growing business and circulation."
"She has a keen sense of humour and is a strong leader with a light touch as well as an excellent negotiator."
Dennis Stevenson, who will replace Lord Blakenham as Pearson chairman next May, said that Scardino had been appointed for three reasons.
Stevenson said Scardino had very extensive experience in the media world and also on the boards of U.S. food company ConAgra Inc and British high street retailer WH Smith.
He also cited her track-record of achieving high quality and fast profit growth and told Reuters she was "superb at managing human beings".

Her record in just over three years at the Economist is an impressive one. The company's turnover has increased from 109 million stg in the year to end-March 1993 to 188 million stg in the year to the end of March 1996.
Profit after tax has climbed from 7.8 million stg to 17.7 million stg in the same period.
